title: Burning and Printing: From Paris 1240 to Vilna
bigQuestion: How did a book that was put on trial, burned and censored become one of the most widely printed texts in Jewish life?

story.title: Wagons in a Paris Square
story.kicker: In 1242, carts of handwritten Talmud volumes were burned in Paris, yet the text outlived the fire.
paragraphs: Paris, around 1242. Carts roll into a public square near the river. They are loaded with books copied by hand, some of them over many months. Medieval Jewish writers later remembered the number as about twenty-four wagonloads. The books are volumes of the Talmud, gathered from the Jewish communities of France by royal order.

Two years earlier, in 1240, the Talmud had been put on trial. A convert from Judaism named Nicholas Donin had brought charges against it to Pope Gregory IX. At the court of King Louis IX, Rabbi Yechiel of Paris and other rabbis were questioned about the book. Christian judges ruled against it, and the burning followed.

Handwritten books were rare and costly. Losing thousands of pages in one day was a blow to scholars across France. Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, a young student who is said to have seen the fire, wrote a poem of mourning that is still recited by some communities on the fast of Tisha B'Av.

Yet the Talmud did not disappear. Copies survived elsewhere, and scholars kept teaching from memory and from other manuscripts. About three centuries later, printers in Venice would set the whole Talmud in type. This chapter follows that path, from fire to censorship to the printed page that students still open today.
story.think: Why might a community keep remembering a book burning in a poem for centuries? What does the memory protect?

lessons.title: The Paris Disputation of 1240
lessons.mainIdea: In 1240 the Talmud was put on trial in Paris, and rabbis were made to answer charges against it before Christian judges.
reading: In 1239 Nicholas Donin, a former student of the rabbis who had become Christian, sent Pope Gregory IX a list of charges against the Talmud. He claimed it insulted Christianity and turned Jews away from the Bible. The pope wrote to rulers across Europe asking them to seize the books. Only in France, under King Louis IX, was the order carried out in full.

The hearing held in Paris in 1240 is called a *disputation*, a staged public debate on religion. It was not an equal debate. The rabbis, led by Rabbi Yechiel of Paris, answered questions before judges who had power over their community. A Hebrew account of the event, known as the Vikuach of Rabbi Yechiel, gives the rabbis' side. Latin records give the side of the accusers.

Rabbi Yechiel's answers, as the Hebrew account tells them, included several arguments. He said the Talmud's harsh words about a man named Jesus referred to a different person. He also pointed to the Talmud's many teachings of kindness toward all people. Historians still study both accounts to learn what was said and how each side remembered it.

words.d: a formal public debate on religion, in medieval Europe often staged by church or crown with Jews forced to take part
a convert from Judaism who brought charges against the Talmud to Pope Gregory IX in 1239
the leading rabbi who answered the charges against the Talmud at the Paris disputation of 1240

look.title: A Mishnah on the Worth of One Life
look.text: Mishnah Sanhedrin teaches that a single person was created first so that people would learn this: whoever destroys one life is treated as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life is treated as if they saved a whole world.
look.cite: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, paraphrased from the Hebrew (the printed Babylonian Talmud gives it at Sanhedrin 37a)
look.prompt: If you were Rabbi Yechiel, how might you use a passage like this to answer a charge that the Talmud teaches contempt for others?

check.q: What was the Paris disputation of 1240?
choices: A public hearing in which rabbis answered charges against the Talmud
A meeting where rabbis voted to print the Talmud
A council that wrote the Mishnah
A school contest between two yeshivas
check.why: The 1240 disputation was a hearing before Christian judges where Rabbi Yechiel and others answered Donin's charges.

check.q: Who brought the charges against the Talmud to Pope Gregory IX?
check.why: Nicholas Donin, a convert from Judaism, sent the pope his list of charges in 1239.

check.q: Why do historians read both the Hebrew and the Latin accounts of the disputation?
choices: Because the Hebrew account is the only one that exists
Because the Latin account was written by Rabbi Yechiel
Because each side recorded the event from its own point of view
Because the two accounts are word-for-word the same
check.why: The Vikuach gives the rabbis' side and the Latin records give the accusers' side, so historians compare them.

lessons.title: The Burning of 1242
lessons.mainIdea: After the trial, cartloads of Talmud manuscripts were burned in Paris around 1242, a loss that Jewish communities mourned for centuries.
reading: After the judges ruled against the Talmud, royal officers gathered the volumes. Most historians date the public burning in Paris to 1242, though some sources give a slightly later year. Medieval Jewish writers remembered about twenty-four wagonloads. Every one of those books had been copied by hand, so the loss was enormous for teachers and students.

Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, later a leading legal authority in Germany, is said to have witnessed the fire as a young student. He wrote a *kinah*, a poem of mourning, that begins by asking the Torah, burned in fire, to ask after the welfare of those who grieve for it. Some Ashkenazi communities still recite this kinah on *Tisha B'Av*, the fast day that mourns the destruction of the Temples.

The burning did not end Talmud study in France at once, but it weakened it. Many historians connect the decline of the great French schools of the Tosafists with the burnings and the later expulsions of Jews from France. Rabbinic tradition, in turn, placed the event inside a long memory of loss and survival.

words.d: a Hebrew poem of mourning, many of which are recited on Tisha B'Av
the ninth of the Hebrew month of Av, a Jewish fast day that mourns the destruction of the Temples and later disasters
a book written by hand rather than printed

look.title: One Book in Many Copies
look.text: Picture a town in 1242 with one copy of tractate Bava Metzia. A scribe spent most of a year copying it. The town's teacher and ten students share it, reading at one table. Now picture that copy loaded on a cart and burned.
look.prompt: What would the teacher and students lose, and what could they still keep? Think about memory, other towns and other copies.

check.q: About how many wagonloads of books do medieval Jewish writers say were burned in Paris?
check.why: Medieval Jewish sources remembered about twenty-four wagonloads of Talmud volumes.

check.q: What is a kinah?
check.why: A kinah is a mourning poem; Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg wrote one about the Paris burning.

check.q: Why was the loss of handwritten books so great in 1242?
choices: The books had already been printed many times
Each copy was made by hand and there were few of them
The books were written in French
check.why: Manuscripts were rare and costly, so burning thousands of pages at once was a deep loss.

lessons.title: Censors and the Basel Talmud
lessons.mainIdea: For centuries censors cut and changed Talmud passages, and the Basel edition of 1578–81 shows how a text could survive in altered form.
reading: Burning was one response to the Talmud; *censorship* was another. A censor read a book and struck out or changed words that church officials disliked. From the 1500s on, many Talmud volumes were printed only after such review. Words for non-Jews, such as goy, were often replaced with terms meaning idol worshiper or with the name of an ancient people, so the text would not seem to speak about Christians.

The Basel Talmud, printed in Basel, Switzerland, in 1578–81 by the press of Ambrosius Froben, is a well-known censored edition. Censors removed a whole tractate, Avodah Zarah, which deals with idol worship, along with many shorter passages. Later printers often copied the Basel text, so some of its changes spread into editions used for centuries.

Jewish readers responded in several ways. Some copied the missing lines by hand into the margins of their books. Later, small booklets collected the censored passages so students could restore them. Modern scholars compare printed editions with older manuscripts to see what the censors changed.

words.d: official cutting or changing of a text before it may be printed or read
a heavily censored edition printed in Basel, Switzerland, in 1578–81
the Talmud tractate on idol worship, whose name means 'foreign worship'; the Basel censors left it out

look.title: Two Versions of One Line
look.text: An older manuscript of a passage speaks of what a Jew may buy from a goy (a non-Jew) before a festival. A censored printing of the same line says an idol worshiper instead. The rule and the reasoning are the same in both. Only the word naming the other person has changed.
look.prompt: Why might a censor want that word changed? How could the change affect the way a later reader understands whom the rule is about?

check.q: What did the censors of the Basel Talmud remove entirely?
check.why: The Basel edition of 1578–81 left out Avodah Zarah, the tractate on idol worship.

check.q: Which statement best describes censorship of the Talmud?
choices: Burning every copy in a city
Printing the text in a new language
Official cutting or changing of words before printing
Adding new commentaries to the margin
check.why: Censorship means officials struck or altered passages, rather than destroying the whole book.

check.q: How do modern scholars find out what censors changed?
choices: By reading only the Basel edition
By comparing printed editions with older manuscripts
check.why: Older manuscripts preserve lines that later printed editions altered or cut.

lessons.title: Bomberg's Venice Talmud
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel Bomberg, a Christian printer in Venice, printed the first complete Babylonian Talmud in 1520–23 and fixed the page numbers still used today.
reading: Printing with movable type reached Europe in the mid-1400s, and Jewish printers soon set single tractates in type. The first complete printed Babylonian Talmud came from Venice. Its printer was Daniel Bomberg, a Christian from Antwerp, who worked with Jewish editors and typesetters. The edition appeared in 1520–23 with permission from the Pope.

Bomberg's edition set the *daf*, the double-sided leaf, in a layout that later printers followed. Each leaf has a front side, marked a, and a back side, marked b. That is why a citation like Berakhot 2a points to the front of the second leaf. Tractates begin on leaf 2, a custom that goes back to these early printings.

Because nearly every later edition kept Bomberg's numbering, a student in Vilna, New York or Jerusalem could find the same passage by the same number. Printing did more than make copies cheaper. It gave readers across the world one shared map of the text, which made it easier to argue about the same lines.

words.d: one leaf of the Talmud, with two sides (a and b); the standard way to cite a page
a Christian printer in Venice who printed the first complete Babylonian Talmud in 1520–23
the system of numbering pages or leaves in a book

look.cite: Standard histories of Hebrew printing; dates rounded where uncertain
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Bomberg's edition and the Vilna Shas? What stayed the same across that time?

check.q: Who printed the first complete Babylonian Talmud?
check.why: Daniel Bomberg printed the first complete Babylonian Talmud in Venice in 1520–23.

check.q: What does the citation Berakhot 2b point to?
choices: The back side of the second leaf of Berakhot
check.why: A daf has an a side and a b side, so 2b is the back of leaf 2.

check.q: Why did Bomberg's numbering matter so much?
choices: It let readers everywhere find the same passage by the same number
It translated the Talmud into Italian
check.why: Later editions kept Bomberg's numbering, giving readers one shared map of the text.

lessons.title: Rome 1553 and the Council of Trent
lessons.mainIdea: In 1553 the Talmud was burned in Rome, and later church rules allowed it only in censored form.
reading: Printing did not end the attacks. In 1553 church officials in Rome ordered the Talmud seized, and copies were burned in the Campo de' Fiori, a public square, on the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah. Burnings followed in other Italian cities, including Venice. For a time, printing the Talmud in Italy stopped.

The Council of Trent was a long meeting of Catholic bishops held between 1545 and 1563. After it, the church issued an Index of forbidden books in 1564. Historians describe its rule on the Talmud this way: the book could appear only if censored, and some later rulings added that it must not carry the name Talmud. Printers sometimes used other titles for the same text.

These rules shaped the Talmud that many Jews held for centuries. Editions printed under them left gaps, changed words and softened lines. The Basel edition was made under this system. The history shows how the outside world could set the shape of a page that looked, to its readers, like one unbroken tradition.

words.d: a Catholic church council held between 1545 and 1563, after which rules on forbidden books were issued
a church list of books Catholics were not allowed to read or print without permission
the Jewish New Year, in early autumn

look.title: A Book Under Another Name
look.text: A printer in the late 1500s wants to publish tractate Bava Kamma. The rules say the text must pass a censor and must not be called Talmud. The printer puts a different title on the cover, lets the censor mark the pages and prints it. Students open it and study the same sugya their teachers studied.
look.prompt: Was this still the Talmud? Give one reason a student then might say yes and one reason a modern scholar might add a caution.

check.q: Where was the Talmud burned in 1553?
check.why: In 1553 copies were burned in Rome's Campo de' Fiori, and burnings followed in other Italian cities.

check.q: After the Council of Trent, how could the Talmud be printed, as historians describe it?
check.why: The Index of 1564 allowed the text only after censorship, and later rules also restricted the name Talmud.

check.q: What was the Council of Trent?
choices: A meeting of rabbis in Poland
A long meeting of Catholic bishops in the 1500s
check.why: The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563 and shaped later church rules on books.

lessons.title: The Fixed Page and Its Frame
lessons.mainIdea: The printed page set the Mishnah and Gemara in the center with Rashi and Tosafot around them, so every reader sees a conversation across centuries.
reading: Open a printed Talmud and the layout tells a story. In the center stands the *Mishnah*, the early rabbinic law code, followed by the *Gemara*, the later discussion of it. On the inner side of the page runs Rashi's commentary. On the outer side runs *Tosafot*, the notes of the medieval French and German scholars who followed him.

Printers set this frame in the 1500s, and it became standard. The layout lets a reader move from a line of Gemara to Rashi's plain explanation and then to Tosafot's harder questions without turning a page. Later editions added more notes in the margins and at the back of each tractate.

The page also joins places. The Mishnah was edited in the land of Israel around 200 CE. The Gemara grew in the academies of Babylonia. Rashi worked in Troyes, France, in the 1000s. A student who reads one page is, in effect, sitting with teachers from three lands and many centuries.

words.d: the first written collection of rabbinic law, edited in the land of Israel around 200 CE
the later rabbinic discussion of the Mishnah; with the Mishnah it makes up the Talmud
'additions': notes by medieval French and German scholars, printed on the outer margin of the Talmud page

look.title: The First Words on the First Page
look.text: The Mishnah that opens tractate Berakhot asks: from what time may a person recite the Shema in the evening? It answers with the time the priests go in to eat their holy food, and then records that other sages set different end times.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, printed at Berakhot 2a; paraphrased from the Hebrew
look.prompt: The Talmud opens with a question and a disagreement. What does that suggest about how the page expects to be read?

check.q: Where does Rashi's commentary usually appear on a printed Talmud page?
choices: On the inner side of the page
check.why: Printers set Rashi on the inner margin and Tosafot on the outer margin.

check.q: What is the Gemara?
choices: The notes of the French Tosafists
The later rabbinic discussion of the Mishnah
check.why: The Gemara is the discussion of the Mishnah that grew in the academies.

check.q: Where did Rashi live and work?
check.why: Rashi taught in Troyes, France, in the 1000s.

lessons.title: Poland-Lithuania and the Yeshiva
lessons.mainIdea: From the 1500s on, Poland and Lithuania became great centers of Talmud study, with yeshivas where students learned in pairs.
reading: As Jews were pushed out of parts of western Europe, many settled in Poland and Lithuania. By the 1500s these lands held large Jewish communities with their own courts and schools. A *yeshiva* is an academy for advanced Talmud study. Poland's yeshivas drew students from far away, and scholars there wrote commentaries still printed with the Talmud.

Students in a yeshiva often learn in *chavruta*, a partnership of two who read aloud, question each other and argue. The room is loud. Rabbinic tradition praises this method; one Talmud passage compares study partners to iron sharpening iron, based on Proverbs 27:17. A teacher gives a lecture, and pairs then work through the text on their own.

In the 1800s, Lithuania became known for a new kind of yeshiva. The yeshiva of Volozhin, founded in 1803 by Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin, a student of the Vilna Gaon, gathered young men from many towns into one full-time school. Later yeshivas in Lithuania, and later still in America and Israel, followed its model.

words.d: an academy for advanced Talmud study
a pair of study partners who read, question and argue about a text together
a town in present-day Belarus whose yeshiva, founded in 1803, became a model for later yeshivas

look.title: Study Day and Night
look.text: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, but thou shalt meditate therein day and night
look.cite: Joshua 1:8, The Holy Scriptures, Jewish Publication Society (1917)
look.prompt: Yeshiva students often cite this verse to describe their study. How does a full-time yeshiva try to live out the words 'day and night'?

check.q: What is a chavruta?
choices: A printed edition of the Talmud
check.why: A chavruta is a study pair who read, question and argue together.

check.q: Which yeshiva, founded in 1803, became a model for later yeshivas?
check.why: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin founded the Volozhin yeshiva in 1803; many later yeshivas followed it.

check.q: Why did many Jews settle in Poland and Lithuania?
choices: They were invited to print the Bomberg Talmud
They were pushed out of parts of western Europe
The Council of Trent sent them there
check.why: Expulsions in the west pushed many Jews east, where large communities grew.

lessons.title: The Vilna Gaon
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, the Vilna Gaon, pressed students to read the Talmud closely and to correct its text, shaping Lithuanian learning.
reading: Rabbi Elijah ben Solomon Zalman (1720–1797) lived in Vilna, today Vilnius in Lithuania. He is known as the Vilna Gaon, gaon meaning genius. He held no official post as a community rabbi. Instead he studied, wrote notes and taught a small circle of students, who spread his methods.

The Gaon cared about the exact wording of texts. He compared versions and suggested corrections where he believed copyists or printers had made mistakes. Many of his notes, printed in later editions, are marked with his initials. He also studied mathematics, astronomy and grammar, since he thought they helped in reading the sources.

Lithuanian Jews who followed his approach came to be called misnagdim, meaning opponents, because they opposed the new Hasidic movement of his time. Hasidic Jews, for their part, stressed joy, prayer and the spiritual leader. Today both groups study Talmud intensely, and historians describe their early conflict without treating either side as the only true heir.

words.d: Rabbi Elijah of Vilna (1720–1797), a leading Talmud scholar of Lithuania; gaon means genius
'opponents': Lithuanian Jews who opposed early Hasidism and followed learning-centered ways
a Jewish movement begun in the 1700s that stressed joy, prayer and devotion to a spiritual leader

look.title: A Correction in the Margin
look.text: A printed line of Gemara makes a statement that seems to contradict the Mishnah it explains. In the margin, a note says the text should read one letter differently. With that change, the line and the Mishnah agree.
look.prompt: What are the benefits of correcting a text this way? What risks might a careful reader worry about?

check.q: What does the word gaon mean in the title Vilna Gaon?
check.why: Gaon means genius; it was the title given to Rabbi Elijah of Vilna.

check.q: Why were the Gaon's followers called misnagdim?
choices: They opposed the early Hasidic movement
check.why: Misnagdim means opponents; they opposed early Hasidism.

check.q: What did the Vilna Gaon care about when reading texts?
choices: Only the stories, not the laws
The exact wording and correcting copying errors
check.why: He compared versions and proposed corrections where he believed copyists had erred.

lessons.title: The Vilna Shas
lessons.mainIdea: The Vilna Shas, printed by the Romm press in 1880–86, became the standard edition of the Babylonian Talmud.
reading: *Shas* is a Hebrew abbreviation for the six orders of the Mishnah, and it became a common name for the whole Talmud. The Romm family press in Vilna printed a new edition between 1880 and 1886. It kept Bomberg's page numbers but surrounded them with far more commentary than any earlier edition.

The Vilna Shas includes Rashi and Tosafot, the notes of later scholars, cross references to the Bible and to legal codes, and short corrections such as those of the Vilna Gaon. Many older commentaries were printed at the back of each volume. Editors worked with manuscripts and earlier editions to fix errors, though some changes from censorship remained.

The edition was so thorough and so widely sold that it became the standard. Most printed Talmuds today, and most digital ones, reproduce its layout. When a teacher in Chicago and a student in Jerusalem say 'look at Rashi on Berakhot 2a,' they are almost always picturing a Vilna page.

words.d: an abbreviation for the six orders of the Mishnah; a common name for the whole Talmud
the edition printed by the Romm press in Vilna in 1880–86, now the standard Talmud page
the Vilna printing house run by the Romm family that published the Vilna Shas

check.q: What does Shas stand for?
choices: The six orders of the Mishnah
The school of Hillel and Shammai
check.why: Shas abbreviates the Hebrew for six orders, the divisions of the Mishnah.

check.q: Which press printed the Vilna Shas?
check.why: The Romm family press in Vilna printed the edition in 1880–86.

check.q: Why is the Vilna Shas called the standard edition?
choices: It was the first printed Talmud

lessons.title: Daf Yomi: A Page a Day
lessons.mainIdea: In 1923 Rabbi Meir Shapiro proposed Daf Yomi, one page a day for everyone, finishing the whole Talmud in about seven and a half years.
reading: In 1923 Rabbi Meir Shapiro of Poland spoke at a large gathering of the Agudath Israel movement in Vienna. He proposed that Jews everywhere study the same *daf yomi*, the daily page, on the same day. A traveler could walk into any study hall and join the class already underway. The first cycle began that year.

The Babylonian Talmud as printed has 2,711 leaves in the Daf Yomi count. At one leaf a day, a cycle lasts about seven and a half years. Its end is marked by a *siyum*, a celebration for finishing a text. Rabbi Shapiro later founded the Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin in Poland, which opened in 1930.

Daf Yomi began mainly among Orthodox Jews, and it remains strongest there. Over time, podcasts, apps and classes in many cities made it easier to join. People from other movements, and some who study for history or culture, now take part too. Supporters praise the shared rhythm; others prefer slower, deeper study of fewer pages. Both approaches have long roots.

words.d: 'daily page': a program in which learners study the same Talmud leaf each day
a celebration held when a learner or group finishes a tractate or the whole Talmud
a Polish rabbi (1887–1933) who proposed Daf Yomi in 1923 and founded the Lublin yeshiva

look.title: The Daf Yomi Cycle in Numbers
look.cite: Standard Daf Yomi calendars; the 13th cycle ended in January 2020
look.prompt: If a student starts Daf Yomi at 17, about how old will they be at the end of the cycle? What would it take to keep going?

check.q: Who proposed Daf Yomi in 1923?
check.why: Rabbi Meir Shapiro proposed it at the Agudath Israel gathering in Vienna in 1923.

check.q: About how long does one Daf Yomi cycle take?
choices: About seven and a half years
check.why: At one leaf a day, 2,711 leaves take about seven and a half years.

check.q: What is a siyum?
choices: A celebration for finishing a text
check.why: A siyum marks the completion of a tractate or of the whole Talmud.

lessons.title: Destruction and the Survivors' Talmud
lessons.mainIdea: The Holocaust destroyed the yeshiva world of Europe, and survivors, with help from the U.S. Army, printed a Talmud in Germany around 1949.
reading: The Holocaust, the Nazi murder of about six million Jews, destroyed the Jewish communities of Poland and Lithuania where so much Talmud study had grown. Teachers and students were killed, and yeshivas, libraries and printing houses were ruined. Some scholars escaped to the land of Israel, America and elsewhere, and rebuilt schools there.

After the war, many survivors lived in displaced persons camps in Germany. They asked for books to study. With the support of the U.S. Army, a full edition of the Talmud was printed in Heidelberg, completed around 1950. It is often called the Survivors' Talmud. Its title page showed barbed wire and a labor camp below, with a picture of the land of Israel above.

Historians note the irony that this Talmud was printed in Germany, the country that had tried to destroy those who studied it. For survivors, it was a sign that learning would go on. The edition connects to the chapter's larger story: burned in Paris, censored in Basel, destroyed in Europe, and printed again.

words.d: the murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, 1941–1945
a camp after World War II for people, including many Jewish survivors, who could not return home
the edition printed in Germany with U.S. Army support for Holocaust survivors, completed around 1950

look.title: A Title Page as Testimony
look.text: At the bottom of the title page: a fenced camp with barbed wire. At the top: palm trees and the land of Israel. Between them stand the words of a Talmud title page, the same text students had studied for centuries.
look.prompt: What story does this picture tell from bottom to top? Why might survivors want a book of legal argument, rather than only a memorial, at that moment?

check.q: Where was the Survivors' Talmud printed?

check.q: What did the Survivors' Talmud title page show?
choices: A labor camp below and the land of Israel above
Portraits of the Vilna Gaon and Rashi
check.why: Its title page set a camp with barbed wire under a scene of the land of Israel.

check.q: Why do historians call the printing in Germany an irony?
choices: Germany had never printed Hebrew books

check.why: The book of the murdered communities was reprinted in the land of the perpetrators.

review.why: Donin's charges to Pope Gregory IX led to the 1240 disputation.

choices: The Talmud was burned, censored and destroyed in places, yet kept being copied and printed

review.why: From Paris to Basel to Heidelberg, the text faced loss and change and kept reappearing.
